OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define SICK scapula syndrome and its etiology and presentation.
Review the appropriate clinical workup for a patient with SICK scapula syndrome, including
evaluation of contributing factors (kinetic chain).
Identify associated pathology and related conditions in overhead athletes.
Discuss the principles of management of SICK scapula syndrome and the approach to
rehabilitation, addressing underlying deficits in motion and athletic form.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
SICK scapula syndrome1
Scapular malpositioning

Inferior medial border prominence
Coracoid pain and malpositioning
Kinesis abnormalities (dyskinesis) of scapular movement
Related to scapular dyskinesis, which is the dynamic manifestation of this disorder
Presents as anterior shoulder pain in the dominant arm of the throwing athlete, often with
dead arm complaints
The characteristic feature of this syndrome is the involved shoulder appearing to be lower
than the contralateral shoulder (because of scapular protraction)
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Rates vary substantially according to sport. In a systematic review of 1,401 affected
athletes, 61% were overhead athletes and 33% were non-overhead athletes.2 A study of
661 elite swimmers demonstrated a prevalence of 8%.3
Disagreement exists with regard to the relationship between SICK scapula syndrome and
subsequent injuries in overhead athletes.4,5 Alterations in scapular motion may occur in
response to underlying shoulder pathology. Whether this is causative or secondary,
scapular dyskinesis is associated with increased shoulder impingement (internal and
external), anterior capsular laxity, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), labral
injury, and rotator cuff weakness.6
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Scapulothoracic articulation (Figure 1)
Articulation between the scapula and the thorax (not a true joint)
Bursa include the infraserratus (scapulothoracic) bursa and the supraserratus
(subscapularis) bursa

Only bony attachment to the thorax is through the clavicle: acromioclavicular and
sternoclavicular joints
Scapula spans ribs 2 through 7; has medial, lateral, and inferior borders.
Suprascapular notch
At the base of the coracoid process
The transverse scapular ligament spans the notch; the suprascapular artery typically is above
the ligament and the suprascapular nerve is below.
Spinoglenoid notch
Below the lateral border of the scapular spine; suprascapular artery and nerve traverse the
notch.
The spinoglenoid ligament spans the notch.
Figure 1 Illustration shows fracture patterns in the scapula. (Reproduced from Zuckerman JD,
Koval KJ, Cuomo F: Fractures of the scapula. Instr Course Lect 1993;42:271-281.)

Biomechanics
Scapular motion
Elevation: trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboids
Depression: latissimus dorsi
Medial (downward) rotation: latissimus, rhomboids, and levator scapula
Lateral (upward) rotation: lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior
Protraction: serratus anterior and pectoralis major and minor
Retraction: middle trapezius, latissimus dorsi, and rhomboids
Glenohumeral to scapulothoracic motion during shoulder abduction is 2:1
As the arm elevates, the center of rotation of the scapula moves superior and medial with
lateral displacement of the inferior angle (lateral rotation).
Vasculature
Subclavian artery
Suprascapular artery: branches off thyrocervical trunk
Axillary artery: three parts; each part has same number of branches as name of that portion.
First part: superior thoracic artery
Second part: thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic
Third part: subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral 
Brachial artery
Nerves
Spinal accessory nerve: cranial nerve XI (Figure 2)
Travels with the superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery
Innervation: trapezius, sternocleidomastoid
Dorsal scapular nerve: C5
Arises from anterior ramus; along with the artery, lies deep to the levator scapulae and
rhomboids, courses medial to the vertebral border of the scapula.
Innervation: rhomboid major and minor, levator scapulae (also C3, C4)
Long thoracic nerve: C5 through C7
Arises from the anterior rami, courses along the anterior margin of the serratus anterior
Innervation: serratus anterior
Suprascapular nerve: C5-6

Musculature
Trapezius (Figure 4)
Originates from the spinous processes and inserts on the scapular spine and acromion
Laterally rotates the scapula to elevate the acromion for shoulder elevation
Has three components: upper, middle, and lower
Latissimus dorsi
Originates from the spinous processes and has attachments to the inferior angle of the
scapula
Scapular depressor
Levator scapulae
Inserts on the superomedial angle of the scapula
Elevates and anteriorly tilts the scapula
Rhomboid major
Originates from the spinous processes and inserts on the medial border of the scapula at the
level of the scapular spine
Medially rotates the scapula

Rhomboid minor
Originates from the spinous processes and inserts on the medial border of the scapula
superior to the rhomboid major
Medially rotates the scapula
Serratus anterior
Originates from the upper ribs and inserts on the medial border of the scapula
Important scapular stabilizer; fixes the position of the scapula to the chest wall, allowing for a
stable fulcrum during arm elevation.
Subscapularis
Originates from the medial scapular body anteriorly and inserts on the lesser tuberosity of
the humerus, medial to the bicipital groove
Internally rotates the arm
Supraspinatus
Originates from the supraspinatus fossa and inserts on the greater tuberosity
Abducts and externally rotates arm
Infraspinatus
Originates from the infraspinatus fossa and inserts on the greater tuberosity
Externally rotates arm
Teres minor
Originates from the dorsolateral scapula and inserts on the greater tuberosity
Externally rotates arm
Pectoralis major
Originates from the ribs, clavicle, sternum; inserts on humerus.
Internally rotates and adducts the arm
Pectoralis minor
Originates from the ribs and attaches to the coracoid
Protracts the scapula
Deltoid
Originates from the clavicle (anterior), acromion (middle), and scapula (posterior); inserts on
the deltoid tuberosity of the lateral humerus.
Abducts the arm
Biceps
Long and short heads originate from the superior glenoid (long) and the coracoid (short)
Depress the humeral head (long) and protract the scapula (short); elbow flexion.
Coracobrachialis

Etiology
Various causative factors
Potential underlying anatomic considerations
Thoracic kyphosis
Clavicular fracture malunion
High-grade acromioclavicular joint instability or arthrosis
Glenohumeral joint internal derangement

Neurologic causes7
Cervical radiculopathy
Scapular winging because of long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy
Typically, alterations in shoulder mechanics lead to subsequent soft-tissue adaptations
observed with SICK scapula syndrome.
Kinetic chain dysfunction
Serratus anterior dysfunction has been demonstrated in athletes in various sports who
experience shoulder pain.
Posterior capsule contracture
Chronic tensile load is theorized to thicken the posterior capsule.
Decreased flexibility of the capsuloligamentous structures of the posterior shoulder results
in superior/posterior displacement of the humeral head.
Anterior tightness: inflexibility of the anterior tendinous structures, including the pectoralis
minor and the short head of the biceps, often results.
Muscular tension is increased after repetitive strain because of increased intramuscular
calcium (secondary to muscle damage), resulting in muscle fiber shortening, which peaks at 4
to 18 hours after an activity.6
Internal rotation and total range-of-motion (ROM) deficits may result.
Altered scapular motion results.

Etiology
The kinetic chain is the coordinated, sequential development of force. For overhead
athletes, force generation begins in the lower extremities, is transferred through the
trunk, and is delivered by the shoulder (arm position, slot) and distal upper extremity
(hand speed, whip). Efficient transfer of force is necessary to create velocity.6
In baseball and tennis, maximum velocity is limited by poor flexibility in the hips, trunk,
and lower extremities and incurs greater stress on the shoulder and elbow.6 Poor
mechanics with inefficient force generation lead to increased stress at the shoulder with
secondary alterations in scapular motion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:36 AM
AAOS | SICK Scapula Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000639
10/24

GIRD is defined as an 18° difference in internal rotation compared with the contralateral
extremity. Total ROM deficit (TROMD) is defined as more than 5° of asymmetry in total
arc of motion. These are not necessarily causative but may place higher stress on key
stabilizing components of the shoulder6 (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Clinical photograph shows assessment of glenohumeral internal rotation, which
is performed with the patient in the supine position, the body of the scapula stabilized,
and the arm in internal rotation to its natural tightness (no overpressure). (Reproduced
from Kibler WB, Sciascia A: New paradigms in the throwing shoulder: Labral injury,
surgery, and rehabilitation. Instr Course Lect 2019;68:499-511.)
Bony anatomy also may contribute to GIRD. Increased stress on the humerus during
development slows natural humeral anteversion, resulting in increased retroversion.
This often is adaptive and may not affect the TROMD; however, it may lead to tightening
of the posterior structures of the shoulder.6
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:36 AM
AAOS | SICK Scapula Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000639
11/24

The scapula protracts and tilts anteriorly, rotating about a horizontal axis, with the upper
scapula rotating anteroinferiorly. The shoulder appears lower than the contralateral
shoulder. The pectoralis minor tightens as the coracoid tilts inferiorly and shifts laterally
away from the midline.
Decreased subacromial space leads to external impingement. Tightening of the posterior
capsule leads to internal impingement and increased strain on the anterior
glenohumeral ligaments with laxity of the anterior capsule (cam effect). A decrease in
rotator cuff strength and increased strain on the scapular stabilizing muscles also occur.
Natural History
Early in the condition, considerable deficits in ROM and form (kinetic chain) may be noted
before the onset of symptoms.
Failure to address these factors early may lead to worsening dysfunction and increased risk for
intra-articular damage.
A shoulder at risk is a prodromal indicator of superior labrum anterior and posterior (SLAP)
tears.1
Tightness in the posterior shoulder, inability to loosen the shoulder
Posteroinferior capsular contracture progresses, and posterosuperior discomfort develops.
A SLAP lesion may then occur with a sudden onset of mechanical symptoms.
Subacromial impingement or radicular/thoracic outlet symptoms may develop because of
restricted space in the anterior shoulder.
Risk Factors
Deficiencies in the kinetic chain and athletic form
Deficits in ROM
TROMD appears to be most correlated rather than GIRD alone (because of limited external
rotation).
Increased risk of ulnar collateral ligament injury and medial elbow torque8
Limitation of external rotation leads to decreased arm slot or may allow the arm to lag while
throwing (compensatory, to maintain velocity).9
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:36 AM
AAOS | SICK Scapula Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000639
12/24

Fatigue of the serratus anterior leads to increased rotator cuff and periscapular muscle
activation and increased scapular external rotation.10
Classification
Altered kinematics of the scapula on dynamic use falls into three clinically recognizable
patterns of scapular dyskinesis.
Type 1: inferior medial scapular prominence; associated with labral pathology.
Type 2: medial scapular prominence; associated with labral pathology.
Type 3: superomedial border scapular prominence; associated with external (subacromial)
impingement and rotator cuff pathology rather than labral pathology (Figures 6 and 7).
Figure 6 Clinical photographs show dyskinesis. A, Type I dyskinesis, with inferior medial border
prominence (left scapula). B, Type II dyskinesis, with prominence of the entire medial border (left
scapula). (Reproduced from Kibler WB, McMullen J: Scapular dyskinesis and its relation to
shoulder pain. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2003;11[2]:142-151.)

Figure 7 Images show type III dyskinesis. A, Clinical photograph shows type III dyskinesis, with
prominence of the superior medial border (left scapula). B, Illustration shows scapular superior
translation on the thorax. (Reproduced from Kibler WB, McMullen J: Scapular dyskinesis and its
relation to shoulder pain. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2003;11[2]:142-151.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients initially describe fatigue and tightness in the shoulder after throwing and an inability
to loosen the shoulder.
May progress to dead arm symptoms with loss of control and velocity
Mechanical shoulder symptoms may develop, indicating a labral or SLAP tear.
Physical Examination
The defining characteristic of SICK scapula is scapular malpositioning, which varies in severity.
The involved shoulder appears anterior and inferior (protracted; Resource 1).
Static shoulder evaluation compared with contralateral shoulder: inferior (dropped scapula),
lateral displacement, and abduction
Evaluate ROM with the use of a goniometer (assess for GIRD and TROMD).
Dynamic shoulder motion (dyskinesis): evaluate for winging with elevation or abduction
(more pronounced with fatigue).
Coracoid tenderness slightly medial to the tip (pectoralis minor insertion)
Scapular retraction test—Manually retract the scapula with the palm or forearm placed on
the scapula and fingers over the coracoid; decreased pain and improved strength with

Scapular assist—Pain with shoulder elevation is reduced if the inferior scapula is manually
assisted in abduction or elevation (Figure 9).
Labral or SLAP tears
Dynamic labral shear test
O’Brien active compression test
Relocation test (pain)
Posterior load/labral shear
Dynamic posterior instability test
Multiple tests required to increase sensitivity
The clinician should always assess trunk, core, and lower extremity flexibility, as well as
symmetry, balance, and strength.

Radiography
Necessary views: AP, axillary, scapular Y
Defines bony anatomy
May identify additional pathology
Acromioclavicular joint pathology: arthrosis, osteolysis, or separation; symptomatic os
acromiale.
Fractures (clavicle malunion, proximal humeral growth plate in adolescents)
Bennett lesion (posteroinferior glenoid exostosis)
Posterior glenoid dysplasia
Scapular lesion (osteochondroma)
Computed Tomography
Not typically indicated
May be useful in the evaluation of fractures or to define humeral torsion
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Useful for the evaluation of associated structures and additional pathology if suspected (ie,
labrum, rotator cuff, SLAP lesions)
Ultrasonography
May be useful in the evaluation of humeral torsion and rotator cuff or biceps tendinopathy
User dependent11
Diagnosis
SICK scapula syndrome primarily is a clinical diagnosis; the clinician should identify
contributing factors and additional pathology.
Differential Diagnosis
Neurologically based dyskinesis or scapular winging
Snapping scapula
Muscle or tendon disruption (latissimus or teres major, pectoralis)

Associated conditions
Impingement (internal/external)
Rotator cuff disease
SLAP tear, labral tear, or instability
Multidirectional instability
Acromioclavicular joint pathology
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is the first-line treatment option for scapular dyskinesis.
Contraindications
Associated injuries with clear surgical indications require surgical management.
Techniques/Procedures
Rest
Activity modifications
Massage
Administration of NSAIDs
Rehabilitation
Kinetic chain
Leg, core, hip, and back flexibility and dynamic strengthening
Combination of movements for sequential activation
Rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer strengthening to reestablish scapular mechanics
Closed chain, followed by open chain
Focus on lower trapezius and serratus strengthening
Addressing ROM deficiencies
Passive and active assist
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:36 AM
AAOS | SICK Scapula Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000639
18/24

Pectoralis minor tightness anteriorly: scapular retraction; results in increase in external
rotation and posterior tilt of the scapula.12
Posterior capsular tightness: sleeper stretches
Proper throwing mechanics
Surgical Management
Indications
Generally reserved for patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails
Because this is a functional shoulder problem, surgical management typically is reserved for
subsequent or associated structural pathology (SLAP tear, instability, rotator cuff disease,
acromioclavicular joint pathology)
Limited, early evidence of improvement in symptoms with arthroscopic pectoralis minor
release in refractory cases13
Associated injuries with clear indications
Contraindications
Inadequate trial of nonsurgical management
Failure to manage the underlying pathology, ROM deficiencies, kinetic chain dysfunction
Complications
Failure to adequately address scapular dysfunction may lead to associated pathology.
Outcomes
Limited data on outcomes regarding rehabilitation for SICK scapula syndrome specifically
Rehabilitation improves 90% of ROM deficiencies.
SLAP lesions often respond well to a guided rehabilitation program (50% asymptomatic after a
6- to 8-week course of management)6 (Video 1).
